standard.title: First Nations custodial responsibility and environmental management
standard.description: First Nations Australians' approaches to custodial responsibility and environmental management in different regions of Australia
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand the spiritual and aesthetic value of landscapes for First Nations Australians (AC9HG8K03) and have engaged with environmental world views including distinctions between anthropocentric and other frameworks (AC9HG10K02). They have developed awareness of Country/Place as a concept in earlier years.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain First Nations Australians' approaches to custodial responsibility and environmental management in different regions of Australia, including the influence of cultural values, the role of First Nations Park Rangers, and First Nations models of sustainability.

nodes.label: Custodial responsibility and cultural values
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what custodial responsibility means for First Nations Australians and identify the influence of cultural values — including continuity of cultural practices, management of Country/Place, and land tenure — on how environments are managed.
nodes.minimum_width: Define custodial responsibility and explain its basis in cultural values for at least one Country/Place with reference to a specific community or region.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how cultural values (continuity of practices, obligations to Country/Place, land tenure systems) shape custodial responsibility across different regions; identify how custodial responsibility differs from mainstream environmental management approaches.
wider: Investigate how land tenure arrangements (native title, co-management agreements, IPA — Indigenous Protected Areas) interact with custodial responsibility in different Australian regions
Research how custodial knowledge is transmitted across generations and what happens to environmental management when this transmission is disrupted
Compare custodial responsibility frameworks in different First Nations regions of Australia (e.g. arid, tropical, coastal) to identify shared principles and context-specific practices
nodes.hinge_reason: If students understand custodial responsibility only as a synonym for 'caring for country' without grasping the cultural and obligations-based nature of the concept, they will misrepresent First Nations approaches in K04 management comparisons and reproduce shallow or tokenistic analysis.

response_modes.reason: Custodial responsibility is a concept grounded in relational ontology that differs fundamentally from both anthropocentric stewardship and ecocentric conservation. Students need a framework that distinguishes obligations-based management (custodial responsibility) from interest-based management (mainstream approaches) before applying it to regional cases.

Custodial responsibility is expressed differently across different regions, Country/Places and communities. Exposure to multiple regional examples prevents reductive generalisation about 'what Aboriginal people do'.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Regional variation in custodial responsibility expressions is pedagogically significant — it demonstrates that First Nations environmental management is not monolithic but is shaped by specific ecological, cultural and historical contexts. This depth supports more nuanced comparative analysis in K04.
success_criteria: Students explain custodial responsibility using the concept of obligations to Country/Place, distinguishing it from general environmental care
Students identify at least two cultural values that influence how a specific First Nations community manages their environment

nodes.label: First Nations Park Rangers and cultural knowledge in practice
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the role of First Nations Australian Park Rangers and how their cultural knowledge and practices contribute to the management of Country/Place and environments.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the role of First Nations Rangers in managing a specific Country/Place, explaining how at least one cultural knowledge practice informs their management approach.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the role of First Nations Rangers across multiple contexts; describe how cultural knowledge practices (fire management, species monitoring, water management, seasonal practices) are integrated with contemporary conservation techniques.
wider: Investigate the Savanna Burning Carbon Farming Initiative as a case where traditional fire management practices are formally integrated with environmental markets
Research a specific Ranger group — such as the Firesticks Alliance or the Rangers of the Kakadu National Park — and evaluate how their dual knowledge system functions in practice
Examine documented cases where First Nations knowledge has changed mainstream scientific understanding of an Australian ecosystem

response_modes.reason: The Ranger programme varies significantly across Australia — arid, tropical, coastal, riverine contexts each involve different practices. Students benefit from two or more case examples to avoid treating one Ranger group as representative.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The integration of traditional ecological knowledge with contemporary conservation practice is a distinctive and substantive topic — students who explore specific Ranger programmes in detail develop a concrete rather than abstract understanding of knowledge integration.
success_criteria: Students describe what First Nations Park Rangers do, identifying at least one cultural practice that is central to their management approach
Students explain how cultural knowledge contributes to environmental outcomes, not merely as background but as an active management input

nodes.label: First Nations models of sustainability
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain First Nations Australians' models of sustainability, including specific practices such as fire management, land care, species protection and community capacity building, and explain how these contribute to broader conservation.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least two specific sustainability practices from First Nations models and describe how each contributes to environmental outcomes.
nodes.typical_width: Explain First Nations models of sustainability including obligations to Country/Place, fire management, removal of invasive species, protection of threatened species and capacity building; connect each to broader conservation outcomes and explain how these contribute to national and international sustainability frameworks.
wider: Evaluate how formal recognition of First Nations sustainability models (e.g. in national park co-management agreements, state environmental legislation) has changed management outcomes in specific regions
Compare First Nations sustainability models in Australia with Indigenous environmental management approaches in other countries (e.g. Māori kaitiakitanga in Aotearoa New Zealand)
Investigate the evidence base for specific First Nations practices — e.g. mosaic burning effects on biodiversity — and evaluate how Western science is engaging with and validating this knowledge

response_modes.reason: This node integrates custodial responsibility, Ranger practice and sustainability frameworks into a coherent account of First Nations environmental management as a knowledge system that contributes to conservation. The teaching signal is to make the integration explicit — not to treat practices as isolated examples.

success_criteria: Students explain at least two First Nations sustainability practices in concrete terms, not just as labels
Students explain how First Nations models of sustainability contribute to conservation outcomes beyond the immediate community
